title: Evaluation and Observability: Evidence for Shipping LLM Systems
summary: Build defensible evaluation datasets, quantify paired improvements, calibrate judges, and connect task quality to production traces and release decisions.
learningObjectives: Design contamination-resistant evaluation splits and representative task slices.
Calculate and interpret uncertainty for paired model comparisons.
Choose exact, semantic, and judge-based metrics with explicit failure modes.
Connect task outcomes, serving SLOs, traces, and token accounting.
Define canary gates and a privacy-aware production feedback loop.

sections.title: Start with a decision and a measurement contract
paragraphs: Say you've built an LLM-powered system, like a support chatbot that looks up company policies and answers customer questions. Sooner or later two questions come up: is the new version actually better, and what went wrong when a user got a bad answer? This article is about answering both. Evaluation estimates whether a system meets a task requirement; observability explains what happened while it ran (think of it as a flight recorder for each request). A fluent answer, a successful HTTP response, and a completed user task are different outcomes. For a support assistant, success might require an answer grounded in the authorized policy, a valid citation, and correct escalation when evidence is missing. Define the unit of evaluation (the thing you actually score) as a complete conversation or workflow when earlier actions affect later outcomes.

With the goal clear, the next step is a measurement contract: a written agreement on what you'll measure and how. Before comparing candidates (the competing versions of the system you might ship), write down the target population, eligible requests, success rubric, unacceptable failures, and decision threshold. Record the model identifier, prompt version, retrieval index snapshot (the exact document collection the system searches; retrieval is covered in the RAG: Retrieving Evidence Before Generating Answers article), tool versions, decoding settings (temperature, maximum output length, and similar knobs), and evaluator version. Together these form the experimental treatment, meaning the full configuration you are actually testing. If you change a prompt and swap in a new document corpus at the same time, the results can't tell you which change caused the improvement. Use component tests (checking one piece, like retrieval, in isolation) to diagnose failures and end-to-end tests to decide whether the complete system is useful.

It also helps to organize what you measure into a hierarchy with three levels: business outcome, task-quality indicators, and diagnostic measurements. Resolution without recontact (the customer didn't have to come back about the same issue) is an outcome; grounded answer accuracy is a task indicator; retrieval recall (how often the right documents get fetched) is diagnostic. These levels don't always move together: improving retrieval recall can still worsen answers if the extra documents distract the model. Aggregate utility can guide optimization, but a weighted score shouldn't be allowed to hide a violated authorization or privacy constraint. The figure at the end of this section traces this path from product decision to evidence.

sections.title: Construct datasets that survive contact with development
paragraphs: Once you know what you're measuring, you need examples to measure it on. Build the evaluation set from representative, permitted examples plus deliberately difficult cases: unanswerable questions, conflicting documents, long conversations, malformed tool results, and rare costly errors. Store input provenance, expected behavior, labels, slice tags (labels for subgroups such as language, customer, or risk level), and annotation instructions. Adjudicate disagreements between annotators rather than assuming one label is ground truth. Keep a representative set for estimating average performance and a separate stress suite for exposing failure modes; their sampling distributions answer different questions.

Next, think about how you split that data. A good rule of thumb is to split by the source of dependence, meaning whatever makes two examples quietly related. Questions paraphrased from one document, messages from one customer, and variants of one template belong together. Random row splitting can leak nearly identical problems across development and test, which makes the test score look better than it should. Use development data for prompt selection, a locked release set for candidate decisions, and a temporal holdout (examples drawn from later traffic) to check whether results still hold as traffic changes. A protected set gradually becomes development data if engineers repeatedly inspect its failures and tune against them. The figure at the end of this section compares these three dataset roles.

A related problem is contamination: the model may have effectively seen your test questions, or their answers, before you ever ran the evaluation. Picture a student who happened to see the exam the night before; a high score tells you less about what they actually learned. Contamination includes exact benchmark overlap, paraphrases, answer keys, and indirect exposure through tuning or evaluator examples. The GPT-3 paper (Brown et al.) documents why training-data overlap complicates benchmark interpretation. Normalize and deduplicate known corpora, inspect semantic near-duplicates, and track access to private tests. These controls reduce known leakage; they cannot prove that an opaque pretrained model never encountered a public example. Fresh private tasks improve evidence but also need representative difficulty and stable labeling.

sections.title: Match the evaluator to the claim
paragraphs: With data in hand, the next question is how to score each output. There are three broad families of evaluators, each suited to a different kind of claim (the figure at the end of this section compares them). The simplest are exact checks, which work best when correctness has an executable definition: schema validity, numerical tolerance, required fields, or passing isolated tests. Normalize (clean up before comparing) only irrelevant differences. Removing punctuation from a product identifier could erase a meaningful error. Tests also need coverage: code that passes three examples has not thereby satisfied its complete specification. If the system calls tools, such as issuing a refund, validate the side effects and authorization separately from the text that describes them (tools are covered in the Agents and Tool Systems article).

Semantic metrics are the second family: they tolerate valid paraphrases. BERTScore compares contextual token embeddings (vectors that represent each token's meaning in context, introduced in the Inside a decoder: from text to the next token article) between generated and reference text, which is useful when surface wording varies. Similarity remains a proxy: changing a dosage, negating a claim, or citing the wrong document can preserve much of the surrounding meaning. Evaluate factual assertions against evidence and inspect numerical entities explicitly. A reference answer can itself be incomplete, so multiple acceptable outcomes or a rubric may be needed.

The third family is the LLM judge: a separate language model given a rubric and asked to grade the output. Judges can score open-ended qualities such as completeness and relevance at scale, but the MT-Bench study identifies position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases (favoring whichever answer is shown first, favoring longer answers, and favoring output from the judge's own model). Blind candidate identities, randomize answer order, repeat with swapped positions, and use dimension-specific rubrics with concrete anchors. Treat generated explanations as review aids rather than proof. Candidate output is untrusted input to the judge and may contain instructions attempting to manipulate its verdict, a form of the prompt injection problem covered in the LLM Security article.

diagram.title: Three evaluators, three claims
diagram.caption: Combine these signals when the task needs all three; no single score certifies correctness.

sections.title: Evaluate the evaluator
paragraphs: If you lean on an LLM judge, the judge itself becomes a measurement instrument, and instruments need checking. It's a bit like testing a kitchen scale against a known weight before trusting it with a recipe; the workflow at the end of this section outlines the steps. Start with a human-adjudicated calibration set (examples where experts have settled on the correct verdict) containing ordinary successes, subtle failures, and difficult boundary cases. Then measure the judge's false-pass rate (bad answers it approves) and false-fail rate (good answers it rejects) by task slice, not merely overall agreement. If nearly every answer is acceptable, a judge that always passes looks accurate while missing every dangerous failure. Include inter-annotator disagreement so the team understands where the rubric is ambiguous rather than attributing every discrepancy to the model.

Calibration has two meanings worth separating. Rubric calibration aligns decisions with expert standards. Probability calibration asks whether items assigned a probability near 0.8 actually satisfy the criterion about 80% of the time. A judge's self-reported confidence is not automatically such a probability. Fit or validate thresholds on calibration data, then assess them on separate data. Version the judge and rerun calibration after changing its prompt or model, because evaluator drift can create an apparent product improvement.

diagram.caption: Calibration examples and final evaluator validation must remain separate.

sections.title: A worked comparison with statistical uncertainty
paragraphs: Now let's walk through an actual comparison with numbers. The first idea is to run both candidates on the same examples, which is called a paired comparison. Pairing removes variation caused by one candidate receiving easier tasks. Consider an illustrative 200-task evaluation: both pass 130 tasks, both fail 30, candidate B alone passes 28, and candidate A alone passes 12. A succeeds on 142 tasks, or 71%; B succeeds on 158, or 79%. The observed gain is eight percentage points, not an eight-percent relative increase. Only the 40 discordant pairs (tasks where the two candidates disagree) determine the binary paired improvement; the bar chart at the end of this section breaks the 200 tasks into these four groups.

To see how much to trust that gain, let dᵢ equal B's binary score minus A's score, so dᵢ is −1, 0, or 1. The mean difference is 0.08 and the sum of squared differences is 40. The sample variance is approximately 0.1946, giving a standard error of 0.0312. A normal approximate 95% confidence interval (a range built so that, under the stated assumptions, it would contain the true gain in about 95% of repeated experiments) is 0.08 ± 1.96 × 0.0312, or about 1.9 to 14.1 percentage points. This interval describes uncertainty from sampling independent tasks under the stated design; it excludes label bias and population mismatch. The formula after this section's paragraphs collects these steps in one place.

A confidence interval isn't the only tool. A paired binary test such as McNemar's exact test conditions on the discordant count: under equal success probabilities, B's 28 wins among 40 disagreements follow a binomial null with probability 0.5. For richer metrics, paired bootstrap resampling helps: you repeatedly draw a new task set of the same size, with replacement, from your original tasks, recompute the difference each time, and see how much it varies. It's like reshuffling your evidence many times to check how stable the conclusion is. Keeping both candidates' results together for each drawn task preserves the pairing, as discussed in Koehn's evaluation work. Resample customers or documents as clusters when tasks within them correlate. Repeated stochastic generations add another variability level. Predeclare the primary metric, practical improvement margin, and analysis schedule; searching many slices or repeatedly checking significance inflates false discoveries.
sections.formula: Δ = mean(dᵢ); s² = Σ(dᵢ − Δ)² / (n − 1); SE(Δ) = √(s² / n); approximate 95% CI = Δ ± 1.96 SE

sections.title: Observe both task quality and serving behavior
paragraphs: So far everything has been offline, measured before users see anything. Once the system is live, you also need to watch how it behaves in production, and that's where observability comes in. A good starting point is service-level vocabulary. A service-level indicator (SLI) is a measured quantity; a service-level objective (SLO) is its target over a stated window and population. Define availability, time to first token (how long until the first piece of the response streams back), end-to-end completion latency, and task success separately. Example targets might require 99% successful transport completion over 28 days and p95 completion latency (the time that 95% of requests finish within) below eight seconds for a bounded workload. These are design examples, not universal thresholds. Include cancellations and timeouts in explicitly defined denominators so the dashboard cannot improve by silently dropping slow requests.

To understand individual requests, you use tracing. A trace records one request from start to finish, and it's made of spans, each timing one step inside it. If the trace is the receipt for a whole request, spans are its line items. Represent a workflow as a parent trace with retrieval, model, tool, retry, and validation spans. Capture durations, errors, route, bounded version attributes (a small, fixed set of values such as the model version, so dashboards don't fill up with unique labels), and token usage. OpenTelemetry, an open standard for traces and metrics, publishes GenAI guidance describing these operations and token fields; pin the convention version because naming evolves. Parallel spans overlap, so summing their durations overstates wall-clock latency. Sample traces deliberately and retain aggregate metrics for all requests; a trace sample biased toward errors cannot estimate the overall error rate without accounting for selection. The figure at the end of this section sketches the spans in a traced support workflow.

diagram.caption: These logical stages are children of one request trace; retries and parallel branches require their own spans.

sections.title: Make resource accounting reconcile
paragraphs: Those traces also carry token counts, which is where cost comes from. The goal here is for your cost numbers to add up and match what the provider actually bills. Attribute cost to all model calls in a workflow, including retries, routing, judge calls, and abandoned responses. Track provider-reported input and output usage, cached-input categories (prompt tokens the provider served from a cache, often at a lower rate), and reasoning-token categories (hidden thinking tokens some models produce before answering) where available. Distinguish subsets from additive categories: cached input may already be included in total input, and reasoning tokens may already be included in output. Record the provider's accounting definitions so dashboards do not double count. Local tokenizer estimates are useful for forecasting but may differ from billing records.

Once the billed token categories are mutually exclusive (no token counted in two of them), estimated cost is the sum of category token counts multiplied by their applicable unit rates, plus other charges; the formula at the end of this section writes this out. Store the pricing snapshot and currency rather than embedding one permanent price. Report cost per successful task alongside cost per request: a cheaper model that triggers retries or escalations can raise task cost. Preserve usage when a call fails after generation, and reconcile periodic aggregates against invoices or provider usage reports.
sections.formula: Estimated workflow cost = Σcalls Σcategories tokens(call, category) × rate(category); cost per successful task = total workflow cost / successful tasks

sections.title: Turn evidence into canary release gates
paragraphs: All of this evidence eventually feeds a release decision. A common approach is a canary release, named after the canaries miners once carried to detect bad air early: you expose a small group of users to the new version first and stop if something looks wrong. Before any of that, freeze the candidate for release evaluation. Require executable constraints, a predefined quality comparison, important slice checks, and load testing before exposing users. A noninferiority gate (a check that the new version is not meaningfully worse, even if it isn't clearly better) asks whether the lower confidence bound exceeds a tolerated loss, such as −2 percentage points; merely failing to detect a significant regression does not establish noninferiority. Rare severe failures need dedicated stress testing and operational safeguards because a small average-quality sample offers weak reassurance.

Following the canary principle in Google's SRE workbook, expose a limited population and compare it with a concurrent control (users still on the current version during the same period). Randomize at a stable user or tenant boundary to avoid crossing treatments within a workflow. Gate on both absolute SLOs and relative regressions, since control and candidate can deteriorate together. Set minimum exposure, observation duration, rollback conditions, and ownership in advance. Delayed task outcomes require waiting for labels; a quiet ten-minute latency chart cannot certify next-day resolution quality. The figure at the end of this section lays out the explicit stop points in such a release.

diagram.caption: Illustrative release policy: advancement requires sufficient evidence; uncertainty can hold a stage without proving failure.

sections.title: Close the loop without collecting everything
paragraphs: Finally, the work doesn't stop after launch. Traffic, documents, and dependencies change over time, and you need a way to notice those changes and learn from them. Monitor changing input mix, retrieval coverage, answer behavior, and labeled task quality. Distribution drift (a shift in what inputs or outputs look like compared with before) is a diagnostic signal, not proof of quality loss: a new topic can be harmless, while a subtle policy change can break answers without a large embedding shift. Compare recent slices against historical baselines and a stable evaluation set. Investigate whether the cause is traffic, corpus changes, a tool dependency, or evaluator drift before deciding to retrain.

User feedback, like thumbs-up and thumbs-down buttons, is tempting to lean on, but it's selected evidence: frustrated users and enthusiastic users may respond at different rates, and a thumbs-up does not establish factual correctness. Combine consented feedback with representative audits and delayed outcomes. In line with the lifecycle risk guidance from NIST (the US standards agency), design data governance into this loop: minimize content capture, redact sensitive fields before export, restrict access, set retention periods, and propagate deletion to derived evaluation datasets. Hashing an identifier alone does not anonymize rich conversation text. Promote reviewed failures into versioned regression tests while maintaining a fresh independent holdout.

interview.question: A new support model improves offline success from 71% to 79%, but costs 20% less per call and produces longer answers. Would you ship it?
interview.answer: I would first establish that the comparison uses paired, representative, contamination-controlled tasks and a frozen evaluator. In the worked 200-task example, the approximate paired interval is 1.9 to 14.1 percentage points, but that does not rule out critical slice regressions or judge verbosity bias. I would inspect false passes, validate with blinded expert labels, and compute cost per successful workflow including retries and longer output. After executable constraints and load tests pass, I would canary with stable assignment, concurrent control, absolute latency and availability SLOs, and predefined task-quality margins. Advancement waits for sufficient delayed outcome labels; rollback restores the full prior configuration.
followUps: How would correlated questions from the same customer change the interval?
What if the judge changes version during the experiment?
How would you detect a rare authorization violation without millions of ordinary examples?
What would make a cheaper per-call model more expensive per resolved task?

pitfalls: Treating a statistically nonsignificant regression as proof of noninferiority.
Randomly splitting paraphrases or conversations across development and test.
Optimizing against a public benchmark while describing its score as clean generalization evidence.
Using judge agreement without checking false passes on consequential failures.
Summing overlapping spans to estimate end-to-end latency.
Counting cached or reasoning tokens twice when they are subsets of totals.
Storing complete prompts by default and treating hashed identifiers as anonymization.
checklist: Specify the task population, evaluation unit, rubric, and unacceptable failures.
Version and group-split datasets; protect release and temporal holdouts.
Freeze candidate and evaluator configurations before paired evaluation.
Report effect sizes, uncertainty, important slices, and labeling limitations.
Validate judge thresholds against separate expert-adjudicated data.
Define SLO denominators, windows, and bounded telemetry attributes.
Reconcile workflow token usage and cost with provider accounting.
Predeclare canary exposure, quality margins, rollback triggers, and owners.
Audit production outcomes and apply retention and deletion rules to feedback.

flashcards.front: Why can a conversation be the correct evaluation unit?
flashcards.back: Earlier outputs and actions affect later outcomes. Scoring messages independently can hide a workflow failure and exaggerate the independent sample size.

flashcards.front: Why split evaluation data by document or customer?
flashcards.back: Related examples share information and difficulty. Keeping groups intact reduces leakage and makes uncertainty assumptions more credible.

flashcards.front: When does a locked test become development data?
flashcards.back: When developers repeatedly inspect its failures and adapt the system to them. A fresh independent holdout is needed to assess the resulting selection process.

flashcards.front: When are exact checks preferable to semantic similarity?
flashcards.back: When correctness has a precise executable definition, such as a schema or numerical tolerance. Similar wording cannot establish those properties.

flashcards.front: Why can high semantic similarity coexist with a wrong answer?
flashcards.back: A changed number, negation, or unsupported citation may leave most contextual meaning unchanged. Check consequential facts against evidence explicitly.

flashcards.front: How do you reduce pairwise judge position bias?
flashcards.back: Blind candidate identity, randomize order, and repeat with positions swapped. Residual disagreement signals uncertainty rather than permission to cherry-pick a verdict.

flashcards.front: Why is overall judge agreement insufficient?
flashcards.back: Class imbalance can make an always-pass judge appear accurate. Measure false passes and false failures on expert-adjudicated slices and boundary cases.

flashcards.front: Why compare models on the same tasks?
flashcards.back: Pairing controls task difficulty and estimates the distribution of within-task differences. Unpaired analysis throws away that structure.

flashcards.front: What is the gain when B alone passes 28 of 200 tasks and A alone passes 12?
flashcards.back: The net gain is (28 − 12)/200 = 0.08, or eight percentage points. Concordant pairs contribute zero to the difference.

flashcards.front: What does a sampling confidence interval fail to capture?
flashcards.back: It does not automatically include label errors, evaluator bias, contamination, or population mismatch. These require separate design checks and audits.

flashcards.front: Why is no significant regression not proof of noninferiority?
flashcards.back: A weak experiment may miss a substantial loss. Noninferiority requires the confidence bound to exclude losses beyond a predefined acceptable margin.

flashcards.front: Why not sum every span duration for request latency?
flashcards.back: Parallel spans overlap in time. Use the parent request duration for wall time and child spans to diagnose the critical path.

flashcards.front: How can token accounting overstate usage?
flashcards.back: Cached input and reasoning output may already be included in broader totals. Apply provider definitions and price mutually exclusive billing categories.

flashcards.front: Why combine user feedback with representative audits?
flashcards.back: Feedback is selectively submitted and satisfaction does not prove correctness. Audits estimate broader quality while minimized, governed data collection limits unnecessary exposure.
